the mechanisms of occupational asthma.
the effects of alveolar macrophage depletion on lung function, inflammation and tissue damage in a rat model of TMA-induced asthma.
the role of AM depletion on TMA-induced occupational lung diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
AMs have a dual role, both in the early and in the late phase of TMA-induced occupational airway disease.
AMs are important in the immediate response of TMA-exposed rats, whereas other cell types are involved in the delayed response.
the role of macrophages in the pathogenesis of asthma induced by TMA is complex, and that macrophages are involved in both the acute response to TMA and in the development of airway inflammation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AMs are not essential for sensitization to TMA but are required for the immediate decrease in lung function.
AMs are important for the immediate response to TMA, but are not essential for the sensitization-dependent inflammatory reaction 24 hours later.
the AMs are important in the early phase of the reaction, but not in the later phase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
AM depletion can be used to study the role of AM-derived mediators in occupational asthma and that AM depletion may also be used to improve lung function in TMA-induced occupational asthmatics.
AMs have a dual role, which is not always in line with the classical paradigm of AMs as anti-inflammatory cells.
AMs are involved in the pathogenesis of TMA-induced occupational airway disease.
